question: What makes giving birth at home riskier than giving birth in a hospital?

options.A: Required presence of a medical doctor

explanation: Home settings lack operating rooms and surgical tools needed when sudden delivery complications arise. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T9#GNS225_U3_T9_h1)

question: Why do community health nurses still assess home birth settings when hospitals are available?

options.A: Traditional attendants refuse to bring patients to clinics
options.B: Cultural preferences and financial factors drive home births
options.C: Hospitals lack sufficient space to admit pregnant women
options.D: Government policies mandate home delivery for all women

explanation: Many women choose home delivery because of cultural beliefs and money limits, so nurses must help manage those risks. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T9#GNS225_U3_T9_h1)

question: What is the main goal of sorting pregnant women by risk during antenatal care?

options.A: Assigning a traditional birth attendant to every mother
options.B: Calculating the total cost of antenatal clinic care
options.C: Determining the exact date of spontaneous labor
options.D: Separating low-risk pregnancies from high-risk cases

explanation: Risk sorting helps healthcare workers ensure that high-risk patients are cared for in fully equipped facilities. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T9#GNS225_U3_T9_h2)

question: A first-time pregnant student with severe pre-eclampsia asks to have her baby at home. How should the nurse respond?

options.A: Delay the decision until active labor begins
options.B: Advise hospital delivery due to high-risk status
options.C: Approve the home birth after checking home lighting
options.D: Train a traditional birth attendant to manage blood pressure

explanation: Severe pre-eclampsia is a serious complication that means a mother must give birth in a hospital for safety. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T9#GNS225_U3_T9_h2)

question: Which baby position is necessary for a safe delivery at home?
explanation: Only head-first, or cephalic, presentations are considered safe for births outside a hospital. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T9#GNS225_U3_T9_h3)

question: Why are women who have given birth before often considered better candidates for home delivery than first-time mothers?

options.A: Multiparas do not experience postpartum hemorrhage
options.B: Primigravidas have a higher rate of prolonged pregnancies
options.C: First-time mothers always require immediate caesarean section
options.D: Previous normal deliveries indicate a lower chance of labor complications

explanation: A history of normal, uncomplicated past births gives reassurance that current labor will likely go smoothly. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T9#GNS225_U3_T9_h3)

question: Which medical history completely rules out a safe home birth?

options.A: Maternal age between twenty and thirty years
options.D: Mild morning sickness in the first trimester

explanation: A scarred uterus can tear during labor contractions, needing quick surgery that is only available in a hospital. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T9#GNS225_U3_T9_h4)

question: Why does placenta previa make a home birth unsafe?

options.A: It prevents the baby from moving into a head-first position
options.B: It causes severe, life-threatening hemorrhage as the cervix dilates
options.C: It stops uterine contractions from starting spontaneously
options.D: It automatically leads to a prolonged second stage of labor

explanation: In placenta previa, the placenta covers the birth canal, causing heavy bleeding when labor starts and requiring emergency surgery. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T9#GNS225_U3_T9_h4)

question: At what point in pregnancy should a nurse check if a mother is eligible for a home delivery?

options.A: After the placenta has been delivered
options.B: Only during the first trimester visit
options.C: Exclusively when active labor pains begin

explanation: Pregnancy risks can change over time, so nurses must re-evaluate the mother at every antenatal visit. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T9#GNS225_U3_T9_h5)

question: What should a nurse do if a low-risk client suddenly develops high blood pressure at 36 weeks?

options.A: Increase her salt intake and monitor blood pressure weekly
options.B: Advise her to rest at home until labor starts naturally
options.C: Reclassify her as high-risk and cancel home delivery plans
options.D: Refer her to a traditional birth attendant for herbal remedies

explanation: A sudden rise in blood pressure means she is now high-risk and must deliver in a hospital to prevent eclampsia. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T9#GNS225_U3_T9_h5)

question: What physical feature of a home is checked when assessing it for a possible delivery?

options.A: Availability of sterile surgical operating tables
options.B: Distance to the nearest international airport
options.C: Presence of electronic fetal monitoring screens
options.D: Availability of clean water and lighting

explanation: Clean water and good lighting are basic needs for maintaining hygiene and safety during a home birth. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T9#GNS225_U3_T9_h6)

question: Why is having a transport plan important when setting up for a home delivery?

options.A: To ensure a quick transfer if an obstetric emergency develops
options.B: To bring heavy medical equipment from the hospital
options.C: To allow the nurse to travel back to the clinic easily
options.D: To transport family members to work during labor

explanation: Failing to reach a hospital quickly during an unexpected emergency can put the mother or baby at risk of death. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T9#GNS225_U3_T9_h6)

question: What is the main goal of setting up a referral pathway ahead of time?

options.A: Providing jobs for local transport drivers
options.B: Ensuring fast transfer to a hospital during emergencies
options.C: Reducing the cost of antenatal drugs for the family
options.D: Allowing the nurse to stay at the clinic

explanation: A planned transport route cuts down delays and moves the patient to a higher-level facility quickly when problems happen. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T9#GNS225_U3_T9_h7)

question: Which of these shows good emergency preparation for a planned home birth?

options.A: Keeping the mother isolated from family members during labor
options.B: Having a clear transport plan and hospital contact details ready
options.C: Waiting until bleeding starts before looking for a vehicle
options.D: Relying solely on local herbs to stop postpartum hemorrhage

explanation: Good preparation means sorting out transport and communication channels long before labor starts. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T9#GNS225_U3_T9_h7)

question: How should a nurse respond to a low-risk mother who insists on having her baby at home?

options.A: Refuse to provide any antenatal care services to the mother
options.B: Ignore the preference and force admission into the hospital ward
options.C: Support the plan while providing education on safety and warning signs
options.D: Report the family to local law enforcement authorities immediately

explanation: For safe, low-risk pregnancies, nurses respect the mother's choice while teaching her key warning signs to watch for. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T9#GNS225_U3_T9_h8)

question: What is the best way for a nurse to convince a high-risk patient not to have a home birth?

options.A: Threaten the patient with heavy fines and legal penalties
options.B: Discharge the patient from the clinic without further discussion
options.C: Scold the family for holding traditional beliefs about childbirth
options.D: Explain specific risks calmly using simple, understandable language

explanation: Calm and clear communication helps build trust and helps the patient see why a hospital birth is vital. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T9#GNS225_U3_T9_h8)
